Validate the following vignette.

Patient demographics:
  age: 37
  gender: Male
  ethnicity: South Asian
  relationship_status: Married
  occupation: Psychologist
  trauma_type: Terrorism
  pcl5: 69

Patient-reported symptoms:
  Triggers: Loss of Control: Lack of control, Nighttime/Dark: Night-time or waking up in the dark, Auditory/Threat: Gunshot noise
  Maladaptive Strategies: Avoid Stressors: avoid anything that could be stressful, Fantasy Escape: I drift off into a world of my own, Substance Use: I drink alcohol, take medication or use drugs
  Negative Appraisals: Helplessness: I can't stop bad things from happening to me, Unrecognisable Self: The person I have become is unrecognisable to me, World is Dangerous: The world is a dangerous place

Vignette:
Arjun Patel was 37 years old, a South Asian American psychologist, married, and by the time he first came for help he spoke about his life as if it had become divided into a before and after. The event itself had happened years earlier, during an act of terrorism that shattered the ordinary rhythm of a day he had expected to be routine. He did not dwell on every detail, but he described enough for the scene to remain vivid: the sudden violence, the confusion of people trying to understand what was happening, and the terrible sense that control had disappeared in an instant. What stayed with him most was not only the danger itself but the feeling that he could not prevent it, could not contain it, could not make the world behave as it should. In the aftermath, he found himself returning mentally to that helpless moment, replaying the basic fact that bad things could break through without warning and that he had been unable to stop them.

Over the following months, Arjun began to notice that night-time brought a particular kind of dread. Waking in the dark was unsettling in a way he found hard to explain to others, even as a psychologist used to talking about fear. A dark room could make him feel abruptly unmoored, as though the room itself had become unsafe before he had fully surfaced into it. He described lying still and listening, and when the house was quiet enough to make even small sounds feel amplified, he would become tense and alert. Gunshot noises were especially potent. If he heard a sharp bang on the street, a car backfiring, or a noise from outside at night, his body reacted before he could think: he would flinch, freeze, and immediately scan for what had happened. The sound seemed to pull him back toward the terror of the original attack, not as an abstract memory but as a bodily certainty that danger was again near. At those moments he was convinced that the world was dangerous, not merely in a general sense but in the practical way that meant safety could not be assumed anywhere.

As the months went on, Arjun’s way of coping became increasingly restrictive. He began avoiding anything that could be stressful, arranging his life to minimize demands, interruptions, and situations that might stir up the sense of being overwhelmed. He was once someone who managed a full clinical workload with confidence, but he started turning down professional commitments that felt unpredictable and delegating more than he used to. At home, too, he became more guarded about what he watched, read, or discussed, as if any extra strain might tip him into a state he did not trust. His wife noticed that he seemed to disappear into himself during difficult conversations. Arjun said that when things felt too intense, he would drift off into a world of his own, mentally stepping away from the present until the pressure passed. He did not present this as a deliberate choice so much as a place he slipped into when he felt cornered by what was happening around him.

He also began drinking alcohol and using medication or drugs in ways he did not like talking about in detail, but he acknowledged that these substances had become part of how he got through evenings and the hours after stressful days. He was not proud of it, and he spoke about it with a weary sense of self-estrangement, as though even his own habits belonged to someone else now. That sense of distance from himself had grown over time. He said the person he had become was unrecognisable to him, not because everything about him had changed, but because the confidence and steadiness he once associated with himself had been replaced by caution, avoidance, and a constant need to keep bad things from reaching him. He found himself looking at his own reactions with a kind of dismay, as if he were watching a stranger live his life.

By the time he sought help, the accumulation of these experiences had begun to shape his marriage and his work in visible ways. The adjustments he made to avoid stress reduced the range of his days, and his wife had started to see how often he was either bracing against the world or retreating from it. He came to therapy not after a single dramatic crisis, but because he no longer wanted to keep living as though danger were waiting everywhere, especially in the dark, in sudden noises, and in any moment when he felt he lacked control. What brought him in was the fear that this narrowed, wary version of life might become permanent. What he hoped for, though he said it carefully, was the possibility of feeling like himself again and being able to move through the world without constantly preparing for the next bad thing he was certain could not be stopped.
